title: os.path.join("/srv/uploads", "/etc/passwd") returns "/etc/passwd" — the base directory just vanishes
assumption: Passing an absolute-looking string as the second argument to a join function is harmless, since the first argument is the 'real' base.

input.description: A filename field a user can make start with "/" — a tar entry name, a form field never checked for a leading slash, or a URL path segment decoded before joining.

what_goes_wrong: If the user-controlled piece itself looks absolute, Python's join discards the trusted base entirely and returns the attacker-controlled absolute path unchanged — a complete, silent takeover of the result, with no `..` traversal syntax required at all.
why: Per the Python docs, os.path.join treats any argument that looks absolute as resetting the path: every previously joined component is discarded and joining continues from that absolute component onward. Node's path.join does NOT implement this reset — it treats the leading slash of a later argument as just another separator and concatenates everything — so the identical call in Node keeps the base directory intact. path.resolve, however, DOES implement the Python-style reset, because resolve is documented to process its arguments right-to-left until it has built an absolute path, stopping the moment one argument is itself absolute.
affects: python os.path.join (resets on an absolute argument)
node path.resolve (resets on an absolute argument)
node path.join (does NOT reset — differs from Python's join)
fix: Never pass a user-controlled string straight into join/resolve as if it were just a filename; reject any value that starts with a path separator (or a drive letter on Windows) before it ever reaches a join call.

test_cases.note: Check whether your join/resolve call discards the base directory on an absolute second argument — the two most common path libraries disagree with each other here.
